evidence.title: RECIPE CARD - TL-5 tank sealing compound (1K PU)
evidence.claim: Step is in the current recipe (RECIPE CARD - TL-5 tank sealing compound (1K PU)).
evidence.quote: 3. Establish a nitrogen blanket on D-4 before the isocyanate addition.

evidence.title: RECIPE CARD - TL-5 tank sealing compound (1K PU)
evidence.claim: Earliest archived recipe revision containing the step is dated 2005-08-29.
evidence.quote: 2. Nitrogen blanket on D-4 during and after isocyanate addition.

evidence.title: Change request CR-2005-009
evidence.claim: The nitrogen blanket on D-4 was introduced in 2005 to prevent pressure build-up in cans caused by moisture ingress.
evidence.quote: Reason: IR-2005-011 (pressure build-up in cans from moisture ingress).

evidence.title: Incident report IR-2005-011
evidence.claim: In 2005, a customer reported a can lid blowing off due to CO2 production from moisture reacting with isocyanate in D-4.
evidence.quote: humid summer air was drawn into the D-4 headspace during the isocyanate addition; the water reacted with isocyanate and produced CO2

evidence.title: Technical data sheet - TL-5 tank sealing compound
evidence.claim: The TL-5 product is a moisture-curing polyurethane where water reacts with isocyanate to form CO2, requiring packing under dry nitrogen (2021).
evidence.quote: water reacts with isocyanate and forms CO2. Packed in 5 L cans under dry nitrogen

evidence.title: Minutes - cost review, 15 October 2019
evidence.claim: In 2019, the nitrogen blanket was maintained because MDI prepolymer still reacts with moisture, causing safety issues with blown lids.
evidence.quote: Keep: the MDI prepolymer still reacts with moisture in air and blown lids are a safety issue

verdict.process_name: TL-5 tank sealing compound (1K moisture-cure polyurethane)
verdict.instruction: Establish a nitrogen blanket on D-4 before the isocyanate addition.
verdict.reason: The step was introduced to prevent CO2 pressure build-up and blown lids caused by moisture reacting with isocyanate (E3, E4). Evidence from 2019 confirms the MDI prepolymer still reacts with moisture and blown lids remain a safety issue (E6).
